clinicalPearls: The most common form of childhood esotropia, typically presenting between about two and three years of age (range six months to seven years), often intermittent at onset before becoming constant
Driven by the neural link between accommodation and convergence: uncorrected hypermetropia forces accommodative effort to focus, which in turn drives excess convergence and a convergent squint

Two main types exist: refractive (moderate to high hypermetropia with a normal AC/A ratio, fully corrected by glasses) and non-refractive or high AC/A (excess convergence per unit accommodation, with the near deviation greater than distance)
Full cycloplegic refraction is essential, and prescribing the full hypermetropic correction is the first-line treatment that may completely control the deviation
High AC/A esotropia (near greater than distance) may need bifocals or antimuscarinic (miotic) therapy to reduce the accommodative drive at near
Amblyopia is common and must be actively sought and treated with refractive correction and occlusion or penalisation
A residual deviation despite full hypermetropic correction indicates a partially accommodative esotropia, whose non-accommodative component may require surgery while glasses are continued
Loss of control, an increasing or more constant deviation, or new diplopia warrants prompt review of refraction and management to preserve binocularity
reference.pathophysiology: In a hypermetropic child the unaccommodated retinal image is blurred, so the child accommodates to clear it. Because accommodation is neurologically yoked to convergence (the accommodative convergence per unit of accommodation, or AC/A, relationship), the additional accommodative effort drives excessive convergence. When fusional divergence is insufficient to overcome this, a manifest convergent deviation results. In refractive accommodative esotropia the AC/A ratio is normal and the deviation reflects uncorrected hypermetropia, whereas in the non-refractive (high AC/A) type an abnormally high convergence response per dioptre of accommodation produces a greater deviation at near. A persistent manifest deviation in the visually immature child leads to suppression and amblyopia.
additionalDifferentials: Infantile (congenital) esotropia, with earlier onset, a large angle and minimal hypermetropia
Sixth nerve palsy or other abduction deficit producing esotropia with limited abduction
Sensory esotropia from monocular visual loss
Acute acquired comitant esotropia, which may require neuro-imaging
additionalInvestigations: Full cycloplegic refraction (for example with cyclopentolate or atropine), the cornerstone of diagnosis
Measurement of the deviation for distance and near to derive the AC/A ratio
Assessment of alignment with and without full hypermetropic correction
Amblyopia assessment with monocular visual acuities
Dilated fundus examination to exclude an organic or sensory cause
Ocular motility testing to exclude an incomitant paretic or restrictive cause
redFlags: Abduction limitation or incomitance suggesting a sixth nerve palsy rather than accommodative esotropia
Acute acquired comitant esotropia with diplopia, raising the possibility of intracranial pathology
A poor red reflex or fundus abnormality suggesting a sensory cause such as retinoblastoma or cataract
A rapidly increasing angle or loss of previously good control
reference.prognosis: With full hypermetropic correction and treatment of any amblyopia, refractive accommodative esotropia has an excellent prognosis with good binocular potential, and some children reduce their hypermetropia and spectacle dependence over time. Partially accommodative cases often need surgery for the non-accommodative component but should continue spectacle correction.
pitfalls: Performing a non-cycloplegic refraction and thereby under-correcting the hypermetropia
Undertreating amblyopia while focusing on the alignment
Operating on the fully accommodative component instead of prescribing and continuing glasses
Missing a high AC/A ratio by not measuring the near versus distance deviation
Discontinuing glasses prematurely and allowing decompensation
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course (Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus)
Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Prescribe the full hypermetropic correction found on cycloplegic refraction as first-line treatment, which may fully control the deviation
Detect and treat amblyopia with refractive correction and occlusion or pharmacological penalisation of the better-seeing eye
For the high AC/A (non-refractive) type with the near deviation exceeding distance, reduce accommodative convergence with bifocals or antimuscarinic (miotic) therapy
Regular review with repeat cycloplegic refraction and adjustment of spectacles as the refraction changes with growth
Strabismus surgery for the residual non-accommodative deviation in partially accommodative cases
Monitor binocular function and stereoacuity to preserve fusion, with paediatric ophthalmology and orthoptic follow-up
